feedback: If a child makes groups OF three for 1/3 of 12, stop and re-share: the 3 means THREE equal groups; put all 12 into three hoops and take one group (4), not a group of three.
If a child reports 3/4 of 12 as 3, they took only one quarter: build 3/4 as three of the quarter-groups - the numerator counts how many quarters to take, giving 9.
If groups are made unequal, point out that fractions need EQUAL parts before any part can be named.
When toggling to the shaded strip, confirm the child sees the same answer two ways (e.g. 3 of 4 shaded parts match the 3 of 4 groups).
activities.intendedInsight: The denominator sets how many EQUAL groups/parts to make; the numerator says how many of those to take - so 3/4 is three quarters, not one piece, and the same fraction describes both a set and a shape.
learnerActions: Put out 12 counters as the whole. To find 1/3, share ALL 12 into 3 equal groups (one group per hoop) and take one group - record '1/3 of 12 = 4'.
To find 3/4, share all 12 into 4 equal groups (3 in each) and take THREE of the four groups - record '3/4 of 12 = 9'.
Say aloud 'the bottom number is how many equal groups; the top number is how many groups I take' as you act it out.
Re-show the same fraction as a shaded strip or rectangle divided into the denominator and shaded to the numerator, to see the continuous and discrete versions side by side.

Check a non-dividing case: with a different set of items that does not share evenly (for example 10 counters into 3 groups), notice the leftover. It means the groups cannot all be equal with whole items, so that fraction of the set cannot be found exactly with whole counters (1/3 of 10 is not 3).
activities.title: Fraction-of-a-set bench: share into equal groups, then take some

feedback: If the child takes only one part for 3/4, count the quarters together: one quarter, two quarters, three quarters - the top number tells how many to take.
If they lose track of the whole, restate what the whole is and re-share it into equal parts before taking any.
activities.intendedInsight: A non-unit fraction is repeated unit fractions: 3/4 is three quarters, built by taking one quarter three times.
learnerActions: Find a unit fraction first: share the whole into denominator-many equal parts and take one (e.g. 1/4 of a strip, or 1/4 of 12 counters = 3).
Build 3/4 by repeating that quarter three times (1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4), counting the quarters taken.
State the link: 3/4 means three of the four equal parts, so it is three unit-fractions put together.
Write the fraction next to the action each time so the notation stays tied to the meaning.
activities.title: Build a non-unit fraction from unit-fraction parts

feedback: If the whole is an amount of stuff and a child makes equal-count groups of unequal-sized pieces, colour-cue quantity versus count and ask again 'same number of things, or same amount?'
Confirm that for identical counters equal count and equal amount coincide, but for mixed sizes an equal count can leave the amounts unequal.
activities.intendedInsight: When the whole is an amount of stuff, fair sharing means giving each share an equal AMOUNT. With identical counters, counting gives equal amounts, but with unequal-sized pieces an equal count is NOT the same as an equal amount, so children must check the amount, not just the number of things. When the question is about the number of objects in a set, the count is what matters.
learnerActions: Compare a third of 12 LARGE counters with a third of 12 TINY counters: is the NUMBER of things the same? Is the total AMOUNT the same?

With a mixed set of big and small pieces of the same stuff (e.g. pieces of food to share fairly), check whether equal-COUNT groups also hold an equal AMOUNT. When the whole is an amount of stuff, amount, not count, is what fair sharing must make equal. Exact equal amounts may not be possible without cutting pieces.
Discuss aloud: 'same number of things, or same amount?' to separate the two ideas.
activities.title: Same number or same amount? Guarding against the count-vs-quantity trap

feedback: If parts along the length are unequal, re-mark so all parts are equal before naming the fraction.
If the child treats 2/4 and 1/4 as the same, count the parts taken: 2/4 takes two of the four equal parts.
activities.intendedInsight: The same share-then-take rule applies to lengths as to sets and shapes, so fractions transfer across continuous and discrete wholes.
learnerActions: Mark a length or strip into denominator-many equal parts and find 1/4 of it.
Compare this with 1/4 of a set of counters: how are the two alike (share into 4 equal parts, take one) and unlike (a length is continuous; counters are separate things)?
Find 2/4 and 3/4 of the same length and notice 2/4 is halfway and 3/4 is three of the four equal parts.
activities.title: Fraction of a length on a number line or ruler

feedback: If '1/3 of 12 = 3' is chosen, re-share into THREE equal groups: each group has 4, so a third is 4; a group OF three is a different thing.
Use the denominator-as-group-size wrong answer as a discussion point, not a penalty.
activities.intendedInsight: Fractions of amounts can be named, matched, and written once their meaning is secure, consolidating the link between notation and quantity.
learnerActions: Match fractions (1/3, 1/4, 2/4, 3/4) to correctly shaded pictures of shapes and sets.
Complete statements such as '3/4 of 12 = __' and '1/3 of 12 = __'.
Spot and reject a tempting wrong answer such as '1/3 of 12 is 3' (which reads the denominator as a group size).
activities.title: Naming and writing practice (recognition and recall check)
